meta.title: Who really said "A mob is still a mob, even if it's on your side"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the historical John Adams. Wikiquote calls it misattributed and ties it to Adams as portrayed in HBO's 2008 miniseries. Here is what he really wrote about mobs.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A mob is still a mob, even if it's on your side'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote lists this John Adams line as misattributed and traces it to HBO's 2008 John Adams miniseries. His real 1774 words: "These private Mobs, I do and will detest."

answer.label: Not John Adams — a line from HBO’s 2008 dramatization
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line under Misattributed ↗ and says it is Adams “as portrayed in the HBO Miniseries John Adams (2008).” It is not in any documented writing by the historical Adams. His own view of mobs is on record in a letter of 7 July 1774 ↗: “These private Mobs, I do and will detest.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Listed under “Misattributed” on Wikiquote’s John Adams page
Letter to Abigail Adams, Falmouth, 7 July 1774

source.excerpt: A mob is still a mob, even if it’s on your side.
trail: Wikiquote lists “A mob is still a mob, even if it’s on your side” under Misattributed ↗. It notes that the line is Adams “as portrayed in the HBO Miniseries John Adams (2008)” and that it “has sometimes been cited as having been actually said or written by the historical John Adams.”

Wikiquote’s page for the miniseries (John Adams (miniseries) ↗) says the series was written by Kirk Ellis and based on David McCullough’s book. That page’s selection of dialogue does not include the mob line, and we could not check the episode captions ourselves.

The Adams Papers hold his real words on mobs: a 7 July 1774 letter to Abigail Adams ↗ written while he was working on the case of “King, of Scarborough vs. a Mob,” which says “These private Mobs, I do and will detest.”
Quote aggregators such as Quotepark ↗ file the line under Adams’s name with no book, letter or date, and Quotepark itself marks it “Misattributed.”
source.excerptNote: No primary source by the historical Adams contains this sentence. What he did write, to Abigail Adams on 7 July 1774: “These private Mobs, I do and will detest. If Popular Commotions can be justifyed, in Opposition to Attacks upon the Constitution, it can be only when Fundamentals are invaded, nor then unless for absolute Necessity and with great Caution.” (Adams Papers, Massachusetts Historical Society ↗)
source.rightsNote: No work by John Adams contains this wording, so his public-domain 18th-century writings do not cover it. Wikiquote ties it to HBO’s 2008 miniseries, and dialogue from a 2008 screenplay would be in copyright. We could not confirm the exact line in the show, so we claim no rights status.

author.name: John Adams
author.kicker: The real John Adams on mobs
author.heading: What the historical Adams actually believed
author.bio: John Adams was a Massachusetts lawyer, delegate to the Continental Congress and the second President of the United States. He wrote often and bluntly against crowd violence. In a 1774 letter to his wife Abigail he called “Tarrings and Featherings” and house-breaking by “rude and insolent Rabbles” things no good citizen could excuse. The tidy modern line “even if it’s on your side” is not his, but the distrust of mobs behind it is.

misattribution.heading: Why this gets pinned on John Adams
misattribution.intro: A crisp line, a famous founder and a hit TV drama: a line spoken by an actor playing Adams was later passed around as something the real Adams said.

items.why: Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section ↗, defined as “Statements originally made by others, that have been wrongly attributed to Adams.” No letter, diary or published work by Adams containing it has been identified.

According to Wikiquote ↗, the line belongs to Adams “as portrayed” in the HBO miniseries. The series was a drama, and a 2008 critique republished by History News Network ↗ notes that its first episode invents at least one scene with “no historical evidence.”
Pages such as Quotepark ↗ keep the Adams credit going with no source. Quotepark itself repeats Wikiquote’s “Misattributed” note.

misattribution.truthLine: The historical Adams did distrust mobs, but in his own words: “These private Mobs, I do and will detest” (letter to Abigail Adams, 7 July 1774 ↗). Even then he left room for “Popular Commotions” when constitutional “Fundamentals are invaded.”

context.heading: Why it rings true — and where it doesn’t
lead: The line sticks because it fits the man. In July 1774, on the legal circuit in Maine (then part of Massachusetts), Adams took up the case of a man whose house a mob had broken into, terrifying “him, his Wife, Children and Servants in the Night.” He wrote to Abigail that “these Tarrings and Featherings, these breaking open Houses by rude and insolent Rabbles” could not “be even excused upon any Principle which can be entertained by a good Citizen” (Adams Papers ↗).

But the real Adams was more qualified than the slogan. He allowed that “Popular Commotions” might be justified against attacks on the constitution, “only when Fundamentals are invaded, nor then unless for absolute Necessity and with great Caution.” The modern line makes a sweeping point that is even-handed about sides. Adams drew distinctions.
detailsBody: HBO’s John Adams (2008), written by Kirk Ellis and based on David McCullough’s biography (Wikiquote ↗), put words in Adams’s mouth, as dramas do. A New York Sun critique republished by History News Network ↗ says the first episode’s tar-and-feathering scene has “no historical evidence” behind it, though it does convey Adams’s real hostility to mob violence. We have not confirmed which scene, if any, contains the “mob is still a mob” line.
